title: Partial frame contracts, SDK handoff and tool hedging — PRD (rough)
content:
Summary
This is a working PRD for an incremental streaming contract that emphasizes small, composable frames for partial results, explicit handoff semantics for SDKs, and tooling-fallback/hedging patterns to provide graceful degradation for tool calls. The goal is to give client SDKs a deterministic surface to consume partial outputs, safely invoke external tools, and reconcile structured outputs even when responses are incomplete or interrupted.

Problem statement
Teams building low-latency experiences need partial responses and guarantees about the meaning of intermediate output. Current streaming designs blur progress updates with final structure and make it hard to safely trigger side effects (tool calls) before results are stable. This leads to two frequent pain points:
- Premature tool invocation causing duplicate actions or inconsistent state when the final result changes.
- SDKs over-simplifying streaming into text deltas, forcing client teams to reimplement heuristics for commit boundaries, error compensation and resume.

High-level goals
- Define a small set of frame types that are sufficient for progressive UX and unambiguous tool interaction: progress, partial-structure, tentative-action, action-commit, and final-commit.
- Provide SDK-friendly APIs that reduce integration code surface: typed frame events, replayable checkpoints, and idempotent tool call helpers.
- Introduce a hedging/fallback policy for tool calls so clients can request non-blocking speculative execution and an authoritative later commit.
- Ensure observability: per-frame latency/cost metrics, tool call provenance, and mismatch alerts for structured outputs.

Non-goals
- This document does not attempt to replace the entire streaming framing work (we remain compatible with existing lightweight frames).
- Not a proposal for a new billing model; uses existing token/streaming billing semantics.

Success metrics
- 30% fewer incidents where customers report duplicate tool side-effects in pilot integrations.
- 20% reduction in integration code size for sample SDK apps (measured on canonical examples).
- Per-request median first-frame latency <= current baseline; 95th percentile tail improvement for committed tool calls.
- Increase in adoption of streaming SDKs (tracked via opt-in telemetry) for production customers within two quarters of launch.

Personas and user journeys
- Product engineer (mobile): Needs stable checkpoints so the app can render progressive previews and only commit actions when stable.
- Backend integrator (platform): Wants to call a safe webhook once the LLM commits a purchase intent, but must avoid duplicate charges.
- Developer building a bot: Needs typed structured output so downstream tool graph can run with code-generated types.

User story examples
1) Chat assistant suggests calendar updates. The mobile UI shows a progressive suggestion (partial-structure frame). The SDK exposes a tentative-action frame that allows the UI to show an inline CTA. The actual calendar create webhook is only triggered after an action-commit frame arrives.  If the commit never arrives, the SDK offers retry/backoff tooling or cancels the scheduled action.
2) Ecommerce flow where a model proposes price adjustments and a microservice should adjust inventory. The integrator requests speculative tool hedging: call the local inventory simulator immediately but mark it speculative; only apply durable changes after final-commit. Audit logs must clearly indicate speculative vs authoritative events.

Contract: frame taxonomy (flat, small set)
- progress (type: "progress"): informal text or percentage, purely UI hint. Not used to infer state or trigger tool effects.
- partial-structure (type: "partial_structure"): a JSONL-ish frame describing a partially-complete structured tree. Each partial_structure carries an incremental schema version and a checkpoint_id. Consumers can render but should not treat as authoritative for side-effects.
- tentative-action (type: "tentative_action"): indicates a proposed tool invocation with an action_id, tool_descriptor, and parameters. This signals the SDK/UI it may present a one-click action. Must be idempotent-friendly.
- action-commit (type: "action_commit"): authoritative signal that a previously tentative action should be executed as the canonical operation. Includes commit_id linking back to action_id and an optional pre-signed idempotency token.
- final-commit (type: "final_commit"): marks the end of a request stream, contains final structured output & commit map. After this frame, the server guarantees no further commits for this request.

Frame-level properties (per-frame metadata)
- checkpoint_id: string (opaque) — monotonic for a stream, used for resume.
- partial_schema_version: string — helps clients understand shape changes across frames.
- causal_watermark: integer — rough token-offset lighthouse for traceability between frames and model logits (internal use but surfaced for debugging).
- provenance: short enum — one of {model_suggested, client_override, system_generated}.

API sketches (server-side streaming wire)
We propose minimal additions to the existing streaming protocol: attach a frame_type header to each event and include a small JSON payload. Examples (pseudo):
- event: {frame_type: "partial_structure", checkpoint_id: "c_42", payload: {path: ["choices",0,"blocks"], chunk: "{...}"}}
- event: {frame_type: "tentative_action", action_id: "a_7", tool: {name: "calendar.create", schema: "v2"}, params: {start: "2026-01-30T10:00Z"}}
- event: {frame_type: "action_commit", commit_id: "ac_7", action_id: "a_7", idempotency: "uuid-1234"}

SDK ergonomics (principles)
- Typed handlers: client SDKs expose typed callbacks for each frame type (onProgress, onPartialStructure, onTentativeAction, onActionCommit, onFinalCommit). Backwards compatible: text-only clients map progress frames to data chunks.
- Checkpoint replay: SDKs can request resume from checkpoint_id. Resume semantics: server will replay the last partial_structure and then continue.
- Safe tool APIs: SDK provides helpers: createTentativeCall(actionDescriptor) returns an object with .confirm() and .abort() that map to the action_commit and a cancel event. confirm() blocks by default but supports non-blocking with hedging policies.
- Hedging policies: client can ask for strategies per tentative action: {mode: speculative_local, speculative_remote, wait_for_commit, delayed_commit}. SDK exposes an out-of-the-box "speculative_local_then_authoritative" that runs a local simulator immediately and records speculative_provenance.
- Idempotency helper: SDK auto-generates idempotency tokens per action unless the integrator supplies their own. This is surfaced in telemetry.

Structured output (schema handling)
- Prefer JSONL-style incremental updates for large structured payloads (partial_structure frames emit delta patches). Each patch should be applied deterministically by the SDK; we provide a canonical patch applier in official SDKs.
- Schema evolution: partial_structure frames include partial_schema_version + a stable schema fingerprint. When fingerprint changes, SDK raises a typed warning event and preserves previous checkpoints to allow developer inspection.
- Validation & assertions: SDKs include a light validation layer with optional strictness levels (lenient, warn, strict). When strict: invalid partial structures surface as errors and tentative actions are suppressed until structure is repaired.

Tool calling patterns and hedging examples
- Non-blocking hedged call: SDK receives tentative_action, immediately triggers speculative_local mode (local dry-run) and emits telemetry 'speculative_local_run'. The user can accept or wait; if action_commit arrives later, the SDK issues the authoritative external call (or upgrades local result to authoritative if supported).
- Conservative mode: SDK ignores tentative_action until action_commit. This is default for high-risk integrators.
- Auto-upgrade: for tools tagged as "idempotent-safe", the SDK can optimistically attempt the action in the background and reconcile on action_commit; otherwise it queues.

Observability and developer tooling
- Telemetry events: frame_received, tentative_action_seen, speculative_run_started, action_committed, commit_mismatch, resume_requested. Include checkpoint_id, action_id, client_id, and latency_ms.
- Debugging console: per-request timeline in Console showing frames, speculative runs, and commit status. Support filtering to show only tentative actions or commit mismatches.
- Alerts: a built-in rule to alert when tentative_action frequency is > X per minute or when commit_mismatch rate exceeds threshold.

Operational rollout plan
1) Implementation spike (2 sprints): server framing support + minimal SDK changes for JS and Python, canonical patch applier.
2) Internal dogfood (1 sprint): solutions-engineering integrates with two internal apps (chat assistant, automation bot) and exercises hedging flows.
3) Beta with 3 external customers (4–6 weeks): opt-in flag on hosted API. Collect metrics and iterate.
4) GA: enable by default with migration guide. Default conservative SDK policy remains wait_for_commit unless integrator opts in to speculative modes.

Compatibility and migration
- Default behavior for older SDKs: treat unknown frame_type as progress/text. New SDKs provide opt-in strict parsing.
- Migration guide will include: how to move from text-deltas to partial_structure, how to use tentative_action helpers, auditing patterns.

Risks and mitigations
- Risk: Customers misuse tentative_action and prematurely execute side effects. Mitigation: defaults to conservative mode, strong SDK helpers, telemetry and opt-in gates.
- Risk: Increased complexity in streaming payloads. Mitigation: keep frame schema intentionally tiny; provide canonical appliers and examples.
- Risk: Observability overhead. Mitigation: sample speculative telemetry and provide toggle for verbose vs minimal mode.

Open questions (for next sync)
- Should we allow servers to mark a tentative_action as "auto-confirmable" based on model confidence? What confidence threshold is acceptable?
- What is the minimal idempotency token shape we need to support third-party tool orchestration?
- Resume semantics across mixed deployments (hosted -> dedicated -> private): can checkpoint ids be portable?

Next steps & owners
- Spike: eng-serving-runtime to prototype frame headers and checkpoint logic (owner: Priya Kapoor).
- SDK: devexp to add typed handlers and patch applier in JS and Python (owner: Liam O'Neill).
- Dogfood: solutions-eng to wire two internal apps and capture metrics (owner: Diego Rivera).
- Docs: product to draft migration guide and example integrations (owner: Ava Chen).

Appendix: sample minimal server event stream (textified)
[frame] {"frame_type":"partial_structure","checkpoint_id":"c_1","payload":{"items":[{"id":"p1","text":"Buy flight"}]},"partial_schema_version":"s1"}
[frame] {"frame_type":"tentative_action","action_id":"a_1","tool":{"name":"calendar.create","schema":"v2"},"params":{"start":"2026-02-12T09:00Z"}}
[frame] {"frame_type":"progress","payload":{"percent":45}}
[frame] {"frame_type":"action_commit","commit_id":"ac_1","action_id":"a_1","idempotency":"uuid-789"}
[frame] {"frame_type":"final_commit","checkpoint_id":"c_3","payload":{"items":[{"id":"p1","text":"Buy flight","status":"confirmed"}]}}

Notes: this is a rough working draft for discussion. Keep feedback focused on the minimal frame set, SDK surfaces that prevent accidental side-effects, and operational telemetry that will let SRE and customer teams understand speculative behavior.
